<reason>A won by making the decisive comparison about allocating costs, rather than preventing abandonment. It distinguished parents’ responsibility for dependent children from a reciprocal repayment obligation and explained why progressive funding reaches wealthy adults without selecting those whose parents become poor. B answered both pressure questions directly and retained a plausible public-budget rationale, but repeatedly characterized taxation as strangers paying while the wealthy child escapes, despite A’s explicit alternative. B’s unsupported 5%/95% assertion also weakened its dismissal of administrative difficulties. A’s comparative case was stronger, though B’s humane safeguards kept the debate competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A used B’s uninterrupted-care guarantee to remove eviction as the distinguishing outcome: the remaining dispute concerned reimbursement. Its comparison between equally wealthy adults with differently situated parents then exposed the limitation of affordability caps—they constrain the charge without establishing why kinship should determine who incurs it.</best_rebuttal>
